2.evidence_source: The present study developed a Brazilian adaptation of the Body Appreciation Scale (BAS) for young adolescents.
2._section_summary: This section reports a single study (not labeled as 'Study 1') that developed and validated a Brazilian adaptation of the 13-item Body Appreciation Scale (BAS) for young adolescents. Participants were 347 Brazilian adolescents (171 male, 176 female) aged 10–13 years; the BAS showed acceptable internal consistency and a one-factor structure, and BAS scores correlated with BMI (r = –.230, p < .001).

3.evidence_source: Therefore, the aim of the present study was to adapt the BAS to the Brazilian adolescent population and verify their psychometric properties (e.g., factor structure, internal reliability, construct, concurrent and criterion validity) in a sample of Brazilian young adolescents of both sexes.
3._section_summary: This section reviews prior validations of the Body Appreciation Scale (BAS) across international and Brazilian samples, noting variability in factor structures and item exclusions in different groups (e.g., college samples, older adults, men with spinal cord injuries). It states that none of the previous Brazilian studies evaluated adolescents and that the present study aims to adapt the BAS for Brazilian young adolescents of both sexes and assess its psychometric properties.

4.evidence_source: Body Appreciation Scale (BAS) This 13-item instrument evaluates the appreciation of the body (love, care for, protect and preserve the body), an aspect of positive body image (Avalos et al., 2005).
4._section_summary: This Measures section describes the 13-item Body Appreciation Scale (BAS), including its scoring (5-point items, averaged, with two reverse-scored items) and reported psychometric support (e.g., α = .93; temporal stability r =.90 among college females; α = .94 for women and α = .92 for men in adult samples). It also notes use of a version translated for Brazilian young adolescents and references prior administrations in college and adult samples; no sample sizes, survey method, BMI assessment method, or BA–BMI correlations are reported here.

5.evidence_source: The researchers requested the permission of the BAS original authors ... to use this scale. The BAS version was sent with the appropriate changes and requested new suggestions...
5._section_summary: This section describes the cross-cultural adaptation and classroom administration procedure for the BAS among Brazilian young adolescents, including obtaining permission from original BAS authors, ethics approval, parental consent, and in-class paper administration. Anthropometric measures (weight/height) were taken individually by the main researcher to obtain BMI. The section does not label any study as 'Study 1' nor report sample size, demographic breakdowns, mean age, or correlations between body appreciation and BMI.

6.evidence_source: “A structural equation model or Confirmatory Factor  Analysis (CFA) was employed to determine the BAS  factorial validity to test whether the original model  provided a good fit to the data.”
6._section_summary: This Analysis section describes use of Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) and multiple fit indices (χ2, GFI, NFI, CFI, TLI, RMSEA) to evaluate the BAS factorial validity, checks for multivariate normality, and assesses internal consistency with Cronbach's alpha (≥ .70). It also notes evaluation of concurrent/criterion validity via correlations between BAS scores and BMI and group comparisons by weight status using one-way ANOVA; the section does not name any specific study (e.g., 'Study 1') nor report sample demographics or numeric correlation/BMI results.

7.evidence_source: For BAS scores, there was no statistical difference between the sexes (p > .05).
7._section_summary: The Results note that sample characteristics are described in Table 1. Male and female groups differed on body image dissatisfaction (DIF = 1.678; t(345) = 4.31; p < .05), with girls wanting to be thinner; BAS scores showed no statistical sex difference (p > .05). No further sample details (e.g., sample size, age, BMI, country), survey method, or correlations between body appreciation and BMI are reported in the provided text.

8.evidence_source: The main researcher involved in the BAS crosscultural adaptation for the Brazilian population also assessed the changes in the items and deemed them appropriate, ... The final version of the BAS obtained from these changes is presented in Figure 1.
8._section_summary: This section describes the cross-cultural adaptation of the Body Appreciation Scale (BAS) for a Brazilian target population, noting specific item wording changes (e.g., Items 5, 9, 10) and replacement/clarification of response options informed by adolescents' feedback. It also notes inclusion of a non-verbal (square-painting) response format and states that the final BAS version is presented in Figure 1; no sample sizes, demographic percentages, BMI data, or correlations are reported here.

9.evidence_source: The BAS original unidimensional model had satisfactory adjustments, χ2 = 77.9 (GL 52), GFI = 0.967, NFI =  0.940, CFI = 0.979, TLI = 0.968, RMSEA =.038.
9._section_summary: This section reports a psychometric evaluation of the Body Appreciation Scale (BAS), including CFA fit indices for the original unidimensional model, consideration of deleting Item 12, internal consistency (α total = .804; boys = .752; girls = .851), and validity analyses. It also reports a negative correlation between BAS and BMI for the overall sample (r = -0.230, p < .001) and for females (r = -0.338, p < .001), plus associations with dissatisfaction indices and an ANOVA comparing weight-status groups.

11._section_summary: This section reports psychometric evaluation of the Body Appreciation Scale (BAS) for Brazilian adolescents, including CFA fit indices (e.g., RMSEA = .038 for the original model and .022 after re-specification), item analysis (item 12 considered for deletion), internal consistency (α = .804 overall; .752 boys; .851 girls), and validity analyses. Convergent validity showed a negative correlation between BAS and BMI for the overall sample (r = -0.230) and for females (r = -0.338); criterion analyses (ANOVA, N = 343) indicated normal-weight participants had higher BAS scores than obese participants.

12._section_summary: This section reports psychometric evaluation of the original unidimensional Body Appreciation Scale (BAS): fit indices were acceptable and Item 12 showed very low loading but removing it did not substantially improve fit. Concurrent validity showed a negative correlation between BAS and BMI for the total sample (r = -0.230) and especially females (r = -0.338); males showed a small non-significant negative correlation (r = -0.105). Internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha) was adequate for the total sample and by sex.

13.evidence_source: The adaptation of the Brazilian version of BAS for adolescents aged 10 to 13 years was properly conducted.
13._section_summary: This section reports the adaptation and psychometric evaluation of the Brazilian version of the Body Appreciation Scale (BAS) for adolescents aged 10–13, finding support for the original unidimensional factor structure and satisfactory internal consistency (α = .804). It describes negative associations between BAS scores and BMI (and positive associations with body satisfaction), notes higher BAS in normal-weight versus overweight groups, and highlights the sample drew from private and public schools with ethnic diversity but no formal ethnicity data collected. No numeric sample size, mean age, mean BMI, survey method, or correlation coefficients are reported in the text.

7._section_summary: This section reports psychometric evaluation of the Body Appreciation Scale (BAS) for Brazilian adolescents, including CFA fit indices (e.g., RMSEA = .038 for the original model and .022 after re-specification), item analysis (item 12 considered for deletion), internal consistency (α = .804 overall; .752 boys; .851 girls), and validity analyses. Convergent validity showed a negative correlation between BAS and BMI for the overall sample (r = -0.230) and for females (r = -0.338); criterion analyses (ANOVA, N = 343) indicated normal-weight participants had higher BAS scores than obese participants.

8._section_summary: This section reports psychometric evaluation of the original unidimensional Body Appreciation Scale (BAS): fit indices were acceptable and Item 12 showed very low loading but removing it did not substantially improve fit. Concurrent validity showed a negative correlation between BAS and BMI for the total sample (r = -0.230) and especially females (r = -0.338); males showed a small non-significant negative correlation (r = -0.105). Internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha) was adequate for the total sample and by sex.

9._section_summary: This section reports the adaptation and psychometric evaluation of the Brazilian version of the Body Appreciation Scale (BAS) for adolescents aged 10–13, finding support for the original unidimensional factor structure and satisfactory internal consistency (α = .804). It describes negative associations between BAS scores and BMI (and positive associations with body satisfaction), notes higher BAS in normal-weight versus overweight groups, and highlights the sample drew from private and public schools with ethnic diversity but no formal ethnicity data collected. No numeric sample size, mean age, mean BMI, survey method, or correlation coefficients are reported in the text.
